name: Romanian
variety: Standard Romanian (literary norm based on the speech of Bucharest and Muntenia)
sources: Chitoran, Ioana (2002). The Phonology of Romanian: A Constraint-Based Approach. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Renwick, Margaret E. L. (2014). The Phonetics and Phonology of Contrast: The Case of the Romanian Vowel System. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
Vasiliu, Emanuel (1965). Fonologia limbii române. București: Editura Științifică.
Pană Dindelegan, Gabriela (ed.) (2013). The Grammar of Romanian. Oxford University Press.
Spinu, Laura; Vogel, Irene; Bunnell, H. Timothy (2012). Palatalization in Romanian: acoustic properties and perception. Journal of Phonetics 40(1), 54-66.
Dascălu-Jinga, Laurenția (1998). Intonation in Romanian. In Hirst and Di Cristo (eds.), Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages. Cambridge University Press.
Jitcă, Doina; Apopei, Vasile; Păduraru, Otilia; Marusca, Samuil (2015). Transcription of Romanian intonation. In Frota and Prieto (eds.), Intonation in Romance. Oxford University Press.
Ladd, D. Robert (2008). Intonational Phonology. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the rhythm class hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
contrasts: seven vowels with three central ones: close /ɨ/ (written â, î), mid /ə/ (written ă) and open /a/ (râu [rɨw] 'river' versus rău [rəw] 'bad'; văr [vər] 'cousin' versus vâr [vɨr] 'I thrust' versus var [var] 'lime')

plain versus palatalised consonant at the end of a word, which carries plural and second person marking (lup [lup] 'wolf' versus lupi [lupʲ] 'wolves'; pom versus pomi; rup 'I break' versus rupi 'you break')
the diphthongs /e̯a/ and /o̯a/ contrast with /ja/ and /wa/ and alternate with /e/ and /o/ (seară, seri; floare, flori)
affricates /ts tʃ dʒ/ versus fricatives /s ʃ ʒ/
lexical stress (copii [koˈpij] 'children' versus copii [ˈkopij] 'copies'; cântă [ˈkɨntə] 'sings' versus cântă [kɨnˈtə] 'sang')
three forms distinguished by final i alone: copil, copii [koˈpij], copiii [koˈpiji]
allophony: word-final unstressed i after a consonant is not a vowel but a palatal offglide on the consonant [ʲ], often voiceless: lupi [lupʲ], buni [bunʲ], frați [frat͡sʲ], cinci [tʃintʃʲ], ochi [okʲ]
final i stays a full vowel after a consonant plus liquid cluster (negri [ˈneɡri], membri, aștri), when stressed (a dormi, a fugi), and when it is the definite article (lupii [ˈlupij], copiii)
/k ɡ/ are palatal or strongly fronted [c ɟ] before /i e/ (chem, ghem, ochi, unghi)
/h/ is [h] before vowels, [x] before consonants and at the end of a word, and [ç] before /i/ and with final palatalisation
/r/ is an alveolar trill with few contacts, often a single tap between vowels
/l/ is clear in all positions; /t d n/ are dental
unstressed vowels keep their quality; /ə/ and /ɨ/ occur stressed as well as unstressed
word-initial e is [je] in the personal pronouns and the forms of the verb 'to be' (el [jel], ea [ja], este [ˈjeste], eram [jeˈram])
obstruent clusters agree in voicing with the last obstruent (subțire [supˈtsire], absolvent [apsolˈvent]); final voiced obstruents stay voiced (alb, văd)
written final u after a vowel is the glide [w] (leu, nou, rău); after consonant plus liquid it is a full vowel (aflu, socru, membru)
phonotactics: onset clusters up to three consonants (strad-, spr-, zdr-), word-final clusters up to three (astm, punct, prompt)
triphthongs with a glide on both sides occur (e̯aw, e̯aj, o̯aj, jaw, jaj, jej, jew)
vowels in hiatus are common in learned words (poet, real, idee); across words they stay in hiatus or the first becomes a glide

stress.type: lexical, free and mobile in inflection
stress.rule: Stress cannot be predicted in full: most words ending in a consonant are stressed on the last syllable and most words ending in a vowel on the penultimate, but there are many exceptions and the spelling does not mark stress.
stress.cues: duration and intensity, with pitch movement where the word carries a pitch accent; vowel quality is not a cue

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; unstressed vowels are somewhat shorter and more central
rhythm.notes: Grabe and Low (2002) measured one speaker; the vocalic index is intermediate between the classic syllable-timed and stress-timed languages and the consonantal index is low.

length.notes: No length contrast. Sequences of identical vowels arise in inflection (copiii, fiii, ființă with ii) and are said as vowel plus glide or as two syllables, not as long vowels. Double consonants occur only at prefix boundaries (înnoda).

intonation.declarative: rising accents on stressed syllables before the nucleus, fall to low on the last stressed syllable and low boundary
intonation.yes_no_question: no change of word order; the stressed syllable of the questioned word is low, the pitch rises steeply after it and falls again at the very end when unstressed syllables follow (rise-fall); when the stressed syllable is final the utterance ends in a rise
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word at the start, then a fall to a low ending
intonation.continuation: rise with high boundary at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: prenuclear rise through the stressed syllable with the peak at its end or in the next syllable; nuclear fall in statements
intonation.notes: Dascălu-Jinga (1998); Jitcă et al. (2015). Ladd (2008) discusses the Romanian question tune, which is of the same type as the Hungarian and Greek ones.

phonation: the final palatal offglide [ʲ] is often voiceless, above all after voiceless consonants

problems: stress is set by a default rule (last syllable, or penultimate when the word ends in a vowel) with suffix rules and a word list, so lexical stress is often wrong: copii is [kˈopiɪ] for [koˈpij], iepure [jepˈuɾe] for [ˈjepure], înger [ɨŋdʒˈer] for [ˈɨndʒer]; homographs that differ in stress cannot be told apart
no voicing assimilation in obstruent clusters (absolvent [ˌabsolvˈent], subțire [subtsˈiɾe], obține [obtsˈine])
the velar nasal is used before the affricate in înger but not before velars (unchi [ˈunkʲ])
some vowel sequences are split or mis-grouped: leu is [lˈeu] with two vowels, leoaică is [leoˈaikˌə] for [leˈo̯ajkə]
the diphthongs of â, î plus i or u have no IPA label and print as 'yɪ', 'yʊ' (câine [kˈyɪne], râu [rˈyʊ]), although the sound used is [ɨj], [ɨw]
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used; the low accent plus rise-fall of yes-no questions is not modelled
good: seven vowels with separate [ɨ] and [ə], and the diphthongs [e̯a] and [o̯a] as single phonemes

final i after a consonant is a very short non-syllabic palatal element (phoneme I^ with palatalised consonant variants), and stays a full vowel after consonant plus liquid (negri, membri) and in the article (copiii [kopˈiji])
initial [je] in el, este, eu, ești, era
r is a trill, reduced to a tap between vowels; written x is [ɡz] or [ks] by word

notes: Romanian spelling does not mark stress and writes both the full vowel and the final palatalisation with i, so a good part of the pronunciation has to come from a dictionary. Moldavian and Transylvanian speech differ in palatalisation of labials and in vowel detail and are not covered.
